title: When to see someone
hook: practice complements, never replaces, medical or psychological care

segments.voice: Yesterday: hard experiences, and the signs that say stop. Your line was know when to stop. Did you write your signs down? Today goes one step further. Day one thousand three hundred thirty.

Open the contacts on your phone. Scroll. There's probably a pizza place in there, a plumber, someone from a trip whose last name you've forgotten. Is there a doctor? A counselor? A number to call at three in the morning if things got very dark? If the honest answer is no, the search may have to start on a bad night, when searching is hardest. This path has spent a week on the honest part of practice. It ends the week with a very practical honesty: practice is good company, and it is not a doctor.
screen: `OPEN YOUR CONTACTS.` → `IS THERE A DOCTOR IN THERE?` → `PRACTICE IS NOT A DOCTOR.`

segments.voice: First, the line. Practice complements care. It never replaces it. A practice can sit beside therapy, medicine and a good doctor. It shouldn't stand in for them. Second, the old texts agree. The Jewish sage Ben Sira, whose book is in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles and in the Apocrypha of some Protestant ones, says, in the King James text: "Honour a physician with the honour due unto him for the uses which ye may have of him: for the Lord hath created him." In the same chapter he tells the sick to pray, and also to make room for the physician. Both, not either. In Islam, a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari reports the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, saying that God has not sent down a disease without also sending down its cure. Some readers take it to mean that seeking treatment is part of faith, not a lack of it. Third, the when. The signs from yesterday that don't pass when you stop. Low mood that settles in for weeks. Not being able to work, sleep or eat. Any thought of harming yourself. Those are reasons to see someone, not to sit longer. In an emergency, call your local emergency number; in the US, you can call or text 988. Fourth, the week. The replication crisis. What held up. Too many good results. Mindfulness without ethics. Mindfulness in schools. Hard experiences. And now this. A week of saying where practice ends, so you can trust it where it doesn't.
screen: `COMPLEMENTS, NEVER REPLACES.` · `HONOR THE PHYSICIAN.` · `SIGNS THAT DON'T PASS.` · `A WEEK OF WHERE PRACTICE ENDS.` · then, large: `CARE FIRST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find the name before you need it. Settle, and let the breath slow. Ask quietly: if things got hard, who would I call? Let a face or a place come. A family doctor. A counselor someone once mentioned. A clinic near you. A crisis line. If nothing comes, notice that without judging it; it just means there's one small job to do. Breathe with the question for the rest of the sit. When the bell ends, save one number in your phone. The bell holds the time.
When to see someone. When signs don't pass, mood stays low, or harm crosses your mind, practice steps aside for real care. Today's word.
Your line: care first. Today, save one professional contact in your phone, under a name you'll find in a hurry. Day one thousand three hundred thirty.

howItsDone: Meditation teachers and religious communities can encourage people who are struggling to see a doctor or counselor, and to keep practice and prayer alongside professional care rather than instead of it.

sources.quoted: Honour a physician with the honour due unto him for the uses which ye may have of him: for the Lord hath created him.

notes: Confirm the KJV wording of Sirach 38:1 and the paraphrase of 38:9–12 (pray to the Lord; then give place to the physician).

Confirm the canon description: Sirach is in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles; Protestant Bibles that print it place it in the Apocrypha. It is not in the Jewish canon; the voice calls Ben Sira a Jewish sage, which is accurate for the author.
Confirm the paraphrase and number of Sahih al-Bukhari 5678 ('Allah has not sent down a disease without sending down its cure').
988 is the US Suicide and Crisis Lifeline (call or text). Safety information; the app may want a localized crisis-line note for other countries.

The warning signs ('low mood for weeks', 'not being able to work, sleep or eat', 'any thought of harming yourself') are general public-health guidance, not a clinical checklist; check wording with a clinician.
